title: Dirty bulk, pure skin: UMG-silicon wafers that getter themselves
idea: Pull CZ ingots from 6N upgraded-metallurgical-grade silicon (directionally purified metallurgical Si, skipping the Siemens trichlorosilane step) instead of 11N polysilicon, then grow a 3-4 um epitaxial device skin. The bulk's own Fe/Cu/C impurities seed a dense oxygen-precipitate field that acts as a built-in intrinsic getter, pulling metals out of the skin at every anneal, so the contamination that would kill a DRAM wafer becomes its cleaning system.
why: Siemens polysilicon takes ~50-100 kWh/kg and is >80% China-made; UMG at ~15-25 kWh/kg cuts substrate feedstock energy ~3-4x and opens non-chokepoint supply. The epi skin plus getter protects the retention tail.

title: Copper, DRAM's worst poison, as its contact metal via self-forming barrier
idea: Replace tungsten bit-line contacts and landing pads, and their Ti/TiN/Ta liners, with a Cu-0.5%Mn alloy fill (PVD plus reflow, no WF6). During a 350 C anneal the Mn diffuses to the oxide wall and reacts into a ~2 nm MnSixOy barrier, so the alloy grows the wall that keeps copper out of the junctions.
why: Removes WF6 (tungsten ~80% China, plus fluorine) and Ta (a conflict mineral) barriers. Cu has ~3x lower resistivity than thin W, so landing-pad resistance falls ~50% or contacts can shrink; it needs Cu-in-front-end retention qualification.

title: Fragile yet fab-proof: solar-thin DRAM wafers riding reusable carriers
idea: Slice CZ ingots with 40 um diamond wire into 150 um wafers, as PV does, instead of 775 um. Each wafer is bonded to a reusable 775 um carrier through a laser-debondable layer for the whole fab flow and released before dicing. DRAM uses only the top ~5 um of silicon, so a wafer too weak to survive a fab travels it as if thick.
why: ~3.5-4x more wafers per ingot gives proportionally less polysilicon, high-purity quartz crucible life, puller time and energy per bit. Carriers are reused ~100x and kerf loss per wafer drops.

title: Memory with no cells: CCD charge loops replace capacitor towers
idea: Store each bit as a charge packet circulating in a short buried-channel CCD loop (e.g. 64 stages, two-phase clocked at 2 GHz, ~32 ns average access), with one sense/regenerate amplifier per loop. The bit is never parked anywhere, it is always moving, and every pass through the regenerator is a free refresh, so there is no storage capacitor and no per-bit access transistor.
why: Eliminates the 60-75:1 capacitor with its ZrO2/HfO2 ALD precursors, TiN plate, C4F6 etch and carbon hardmask, and the per-cell transistor. Gates alone give ~3-4F2 per bit; clock power is the main risk.

title: Junctions without dopants: work-function-induced charge-plasma access transistors
idea: Form the access transistor's source and drain electrostatically. Low-work-function (~4.1 eV) and high-work-function (~4.8 eV) contact metals on undoped ultrathin silicon induce electron- and hole-plasma regions, so the n+ regions exist only as fields: a diode with no dopants.
why: Removes AsH3/PH3/B2H6 toxic hydride gases, ion implanters (~10% of front-end tool capital, energy-heavy) and ~1000 C activation anneals. Removing random dopant fluctuation and implant damage also trims the junction-leakage tail behind refresh.

title: Greenhouse gas kills forever-chemicals: CO2 boils inside etch chucks
idea: Replace the PFPE/hydrofluoroether (Galden, Novec-type) chiller loops that hold cryo and high-aspect-ratio etch chucks at -20 to -60 C with direct two-phase CO2 (R744) evaporation in micro-channels machined into the chuck base. Boiling CO2 removes heat at constant temperature with roughly 10x the heat-transfer coefficient of single-phase PFPE.
why: 3M's exit from PFAS made PFPE heat-transfer fluids a fresh chokepoint. CO2 has GWP 1 versus ~10,000, is ubiquitous and cheap, and isothermal boiling tightens wafer temperature uniformity; fluid charge per chiller drops ~90%.

title: Continuous fab, intermittent power: WIP queues as the plant's battery
idea: Split the flow into energy-heavy steps (epi, furnaces, CVD, anneals, EUV) and light steps, and buffer 2-3 days of WIP between them. Heavy tools throttle to follow wind/solar surplus and cheap-price hours while light steps run flat, so the inventory of half-made wafers stores the energy-time shift a battery would.
why: Fabs are 100-300 MW baseload; shifting ~30% of load to surplus hours cuts energy cost ~20-35% and avoids firm-capacity grid builds that delay new U.S. fabs. The cost is extra WIP carrying capital, ~1-2% of wafer cost.

title: Polycrystalline wafer, single-crystal skin: zone-melted device layer on cast silicon
idea: Cast cheap multicrystalline silicon sheets straight from the melt on a cooled, nitride-coated die (no CZ puller, no saw). Then cap with oxide, deposit polysilicon and zone-melt-recrystallize it laterally from seed windows into a single-crystal device layer only ~1-2 um thick, because crystal perfection is needed where the cells are, not under them.
why: Avoids CZ pulling, Spruce Pine high-purity quartz crucibles (>80% share) and ~40% wire-saw kerf; cast sheet energy is ~1/3 of CZ plus wafering. The SOI-like skin also cuts junction leakage.

title: Silicon floats on itself: single-crystal sheets skimmed off the melt
idea: Exploit the ice-like paradox that solid silicon is ~10% less dense than liquid silicon. Grow a thin single-crystal sheet horizontally on the melt surface by cooling a strip of the surface (floating-silicon method) and pull it off continuously as a kerfless ~200-300 um ribbon to cut into DRAM substrates, with no ingot and no sawing.
why: Removes wire-saw kerf (~40% of silicon) and the ingot-pulling energy per wafer, and stretches each crucible over a continuous run, cutting quartz and polysilicon per bit ~2x. The challenge is DRAM-grade defect density.

title: Memory built to forget: millisecond-retention tier needs no high-k pillars
idea: Add a DRAM tier specified for only ~1 ms retention at 85 C, where the runtime places only short-lived data (activations, KV-cache scratch, network buffers, GC nurseries) and refreshes only live pages. With retention relaxed 64x, a planar or shallow-trench SiO2/Si3N4 capacitor of ~0.5-1 fF on short bit-lines suffices, so the forgetting is the spec, not a defect.
why: For a large share of bits it removes HfO2/ZrO2 ALD, TiN plates, 60-75:1 capacitor etch with its fluorocarbon gases, and the carbon hardmask. The cell process nears logic-fab simplicity, cutting capacitor-module cost and materials ~70%.

title: Spent acid as fresh oxidizer: electrolytic recharging of sulfuric strip baths
idea: Instead of buying H2O2 and dumping sulfuric-peroxide resist-strip baths every few hours, loop the used sulfuric acid through a boron-doped-diamond-anode electrolysis cell at the tool. The cell oxidizes sulfate back into peroxodisulfate, the active stripping species, so the 'waste' bath is recharged like a battery and only bled for dissolved metals.
why: SPM strips are the largest wet-chemical volume in a DRAM fab (one after every implant and litho rework). Sulfuric purchase and neutralization waste fall ~80-90% and H2O2 disappears entirely.

title: Dirty steam, ultrapure rinse: the wafer is the still's condenser
idea: Rinse wafers with steam raised from ordinary reverse-osmosis water flowing over a wafer held ~20 C cooler, so a continuously renewed film of freshly distilled condensate forms, sweeps residue off the edge and drains: vapor degreasing applied to water rinsing. Distillation happens on the wafer itself, so the plant supplies only RO-grade water and condensate volume is ~1/20 of a spray rinse.
why: Targets ultrapure-water volume and plant capital (mixed-bed resins, UF, degassing) with a claimed ~80-90% cut in rinse water; steam can come from fab waste heat. Volatile carry-over (CO2, NH3, light organics) must be stripped.

title: Rinse water becomes the etchant: hydrothermal removal of oxide molds
idea: Remove sacrificial SiO2 capacitor molds and other sacrificial oxides with near-critical water (~350 C, ~20 MPa, trace NH3 mineralizer) instead of HF or buffered oxide etch, using the same chemistry nature uses to dissolve and regrow quartz. The dissolved silica precipitates on cooling and is filtered out as pure SiO2.
why: Eliminates HF/NH4F purchase and fluoride wastewater (CaF2 sludge). The near-zero surface tension near the critical point also spares tall pillars without a separate dry. Selectivity to TiN/SiN supports must be proven.

title: One wafer, two fronts: DRAM arrays built on both faces
idea: Run front-end high-temperature steps on both polished faces alternately (flip-chucked on edge-exclusion pins with a protective cap), then build arrays and metal on both sides, joined by a few hundred through-wafer power/IO vias at the die edge. Each wafer start yields two back-to-back dies, because the 'back side' is just a front nobody used.
why: Halves polysilicon, crucible and pulling energy per bit and doubles bits per wafer start without bonding or thinning. Costs extra handling and a double thermal budget, offset by interleaving the hot steps.

title: Vacuum process without vacuum: atmospheric microplasma arrays for strips
idea: Do resist ashing, carbon-hardmask removal and isotropic etches with dense arrays of micro-hollow-cathode discharges at atmospheric pressure, where sub-mm gaps keep the plasma cold and stable. The wafer scans under the array like an inkjet head, with no load-locks, turbo or dry pumps.
why: Vacuum pumping and its abatement are ~20-30% of tool electricity; removing them from ~15% of steps cuts fab energy several percent and tool capital. ~100x higher radical flux shortens process time.

title: Weakest metal in the deepest trench: aluminum wordlines filled last
idea: Build buried-wordline trenches around a sacrificial nitride placeholder, finish every high-temperature step, and only then exhume the placeholder through edge slits (as in 3D-NAND replacement gate). Refill with CVD aluminum from dimethylaluminum hydride over a thin work-function liner, so the lowest-melting metal sits where the hottest steps happen by arriving after them.
why: Removes tungsten (~80% China) and WF6 from the wordline. Bulk Al resistivity of 2.7 versus ~5.3 uOhm-cm for W allows thinner, lower-RC wordlines and lower drive voltage, and aluminum is refined domestically.

title: Insulator made denser by conductor: metal-island percolation dielectric capacitors
idea: Build the capacitor dielectric as an Al2O3 or SiO2 matrix loaded with isolated 1-2 nm aluminum or TiN nano-islands (sub-monolayer metal cycles in a nanolaminate) tuned just below the percolation threshold. Near percolation the effective permittivity climbs steeply to k 50-100+ as islands form a dense series-parallel micro-capacitor network: conductors make the insulator better.
why: High-k without Hf/Zr, from abundant Al, Si, O and Ti. k~70 relaxes the capacitor aspect ratio from ~70:1 toward ~40:1 (fact 1), cutting etch-gas and hardmask use. Leakage near percolation is the risk.

title: Chaos as purity: entropy-stabilized rock-salt oxide dielectrics tolerate dirty precursors
idea: Deposit a (Mg,Ni,Cu,Zn,Fe)O high-entropy rock-salt oxide as the cell dielectric. Five abundant cations share one lattice at random, stabilized by configurational entropy, and the reported giant permittivity comes from that disorder, so a stray extra percent of a cation is not an impurity, just a sixth component.
why: Replaces hafnium and zirconium (byproducts of nuclear-zirconium separation) with abundant elements, widens precursor purity tolerance (cheaper, domestic sources) and targets k>60 at 5 nm. Whether the permittivity survives at ns speeds is the risk.

title: Wafers born with capacitors: eutectic Si-TiSi2 ingots grow pillar arrays
idea: Directionally solidify a Si-TiSi2 eutectic fast enough that the silicide freezes as billions of parallel nanorods at ~100 nm pitch (pitch set by lambda^2*v = const) running through the silicon. Slicing across the growth axis gives wafers already threaded with vertical metal rods, which a short selective silicon recess turns into tall storage electrodes or buried vias: the melt self-organizes what plasma etch carves.
why: Eliminates high-aspect-ratio hole etch (C4F6/C4F8, carbon hardmask, a critical litho layer) and pillar collapse; Ti is abundant. Rods are quasi-periodic, so cells must self-align to them.

title: Dirtier chemicals, same yield: spike tests to right-size every purity spec
idea: Run deliberate contamination-spiking experiments per process step, dosing Fe, Na, Cu, particles and TOC into each wet chemical and gas at 3x, 10x and 100x spec on short loops with retention-tail readout. This maps which of the ~300 chemical and gas specs actually move DRAM retention and yield; insensitive ones are relaxed one SEMI grade and second-sourced from non-chokepoint suppliers.
why: Ultra-high-purity grades cost 2-10x more and come from few suppliers. Relaxing 30-50% of specs cuts chemical cost and the energy and water of purification ~20-40%, and widens the U.S. supplier base.

title: Cleanest factory fed by the dirtiest: fab, chlor-alkali, desalination campus
idea: Co-site a DRAM fab with a membrane chlor-alkali plant and a desalination plant. Chlor-alkali pipes over hydrogen, chlorine (for etch and HCl synthesis) and NaOH (for acid and fluoride waste neutralization), purified desal brine feeds the chlor-alkali cells, and desal water plus fab waste heat close the water loop.
why: Removes cylinder and truck logistics for H2, Cl2, HCl and caustic at commodity pipeline prices. Desal water frees fabs from stressed aquifers (Arizona, Taiwan); water and chemical cost fall ~20-30%.

title: Sand straight to transistor: molten-salt electrodeposited silicon on graphite foil
idea: Electrodeposit dense crystalline silicon films (2-5 um) at ~850 C from SiO2 dissolved in molten CaCl2/CaO directly onto graphite or nickel-alloy foil, so the electrolysis that reduces sand is also the deposition. The film is then laser-annealed for large grains and used for thin-film gain cells and periphery: a dirty salt bath yields device silicon because the electrode potential window rejects other metals.
why: Skips carbothermic MG-Si, Siemens polysilicon, CZ pulling, quartz crucibles and wafering, with silicon energy ~10-15 kWh/kg versus >100. Reported film purity of ~5-6N suits thin-film devices on a non-silicon substrate.

title: The substrate is the capacitor: dealloyed nanoporous copper foil plates
idea: Use a Cu-Mn (or Cu-Al) alloy foil as the substrate and selectively dissolve the Mn/Al from its top 1-2 um so the remaining copper self-organizes into a ~20 nm-ligament sponge with 50-100x surface area. Coat it conformally with dielectric and a per-cell patterned top electrode, so the foil is the common plate of every cell capacitor: removing metal creates more electrode.
why: Replaces the etched 60-75:1 pillar capacitor (fluorocarbon etch, carbon hardmask, TiN) with abundant metal and wet chemistry on a non-silicon substrate. Thin-film transistors sit above a planarizer.

title: One unsorted nanotube film is both wire and switch
idea: Coat polyimide or steel foil with an unsorted carbon-nanotube network (~1/3 metallic) instead of paying for chirality sorting. Under gates, a gate-off high-current pulse burns the metallic paths open so the film becomes a semiconducting channel; outside gates the same metallic tubes are kept as local interconnect, so the 'contaminant' tubes become the wiring.
why: Carbon from methane or CO2 is abundant and U.S.-producible, at <300 C on foil with no wafer, no W plugs and no doped silicon. Skipping sorting cuts CNT cost ~10x; access-device leakage is the risk.

title: Grow on table salt, release with water: dissolvable NaCl substrates
idea: Build thin-film memory layers on polished, cleaved rock-salt (NaCl) plates capped by a sputtered Si3N4/Al2O3 sodium barrier, keeping every step below ~550 C. At the end, bond the film to its final carrier and dissolve the salt in water, recrystallizing it into new plates. Sodium, the classic MOS killer, becomes the carrier.
why: Substrate cost is cents and endlessly recyclable, with no CZ, quartz or polysilicon; salt is abundant and domestic. Risks are Na migration, ~40 ppm/K expansion mismatch and humidity handling.

title: Memory grown on the heat spreader: hottest part carries steadiest bits
idea: Deposit a planarizing dielectric and thin-film memory arrays directly on the inner face of the processor's copper lid, wired down to the processor through micro-bumps in the thermal-interface area. The lid replaces both the DRAM wafer and the ABF build-up substrate, and its huge thermal mass holds the array at a hot but steady temperature, so refresh is tuned to one narrow window instead of a worst case.
why: Removes the silicon wafer and ABF film (one supplier, ~95% share) for near-processor memory. Millimetre links cut data-movement energy toward ~0.3 pJ/bit (fact 5).

title: Grown, not carved: tin-seeded silicon nanowire access transistors on foil
idea: Print tin dots on an oxide-coated metal foil and grow vertical silicon nanowires by vapor-liquid-solid growth from SiH4 at 400-500 C, each wire becoming a gate-all-around vertical access transistor with its capacitor stacked on the tip: a liquid droplet, not a wafer, supplies crystal perfection. Tin is isovalent with silicon, so leftover catalyst forms no deep traps, unlike gold.
why: Single-crystal channels with no silicon wafer, CZ, quartz or channel etch, and no scarce gold catalyst. A vertical cell reaches ~4F2 at coarse litho.

title: Mined mineral, atomically perfect: cleave-renewed mica substrate decks
idea: Use thick natural muscovite blocks (already a byproduct of the same pegmatite mining as high-purity quartz) as van der Waals substrates: grow crystalline device films by vdW epitaxy, which tolerates lattice mismatch, then release them by water intercalation. Cleave a fresh atomically flat face for the next run, so a 1 mm block yields hundreds of perfect surfaces.
why: Gives a single-crystal-quality substrate with no crystal-growth energy, CZ or wafering; cost per surface is cents. Limits are the ~600 C dehydroxylation ceiling and ~10-15 cm sheets.

title: Spinning storage becomes still memory: hard-disk platters as substrates
idea: Build thin-film memory on superpolished NiP-plated aluminum hard-disk platters (~0.1 nm roughness, flatter than prime wafers, made by the hundreds of millions at a few dollars each), using the existing disk-media sputter lines for barrier and electrode films and keeping steps below NiP crystallization (~300 C). A shrinking storage industry's substrate chain becomes memory capacity.
why: Adds an instant, already-scaled non-silicon substrate base with no polysilicon, CZ or quartz, at ~10x lower cost per cm2 than wafers, plus idle media capacity in Asia and the U.S. Low-temperature devices are required.

title: Build it big, draw it small: memory fiber sliced into dies
idea: Assemble a 3 cm polymer-clad preform holding millimetre-scale electrode, dielectric and chalcogenide-channel layers laid out as thousands of parallel cell cross-sections, then thermally draw it 1000x into kilometres of fiber that keeps the layout at ~100 nm. Slice the fiber crosswise into discs so each slice is a die, with resolution set by the draw ratio and capacitor height by slice thickness, so a 100:1 aspect ratio comes free.
why: No EUV/ArF patterning, wafer or crucible; one preform yields millions of dies, and a draw tower costs ~$1-5M versus a $15B fab. Capillary breakup below 1 um is the risk.

title: Delamination as construction: stressed films self-roll into Swiss-roll capacitors
idea: Deposit a planar stack (release layer, strained SiNx bilayer, electrode, dielectric, electrode) on metal foil or ceramic, then dissolve the release layer so built-in stress curls each pad into a 10-40-turn microtube. A flat strip becomes a 20-40x-area capacitor: the film stress engineers usually fight becomes the 3D tool.
why: High capacitance without high-aspect-ratio etch, fluorocarbons, carbon hardmask or hafnium (a thicker cheap dielectric works). The footprint suits embedded and near-memory arrays.

title: Coarse sheet, dense block: accordion-folded thin-film memory webs
idea: Make a single-layer thin-film memory on a 5 um polyimide or stainless-steel web at 1 um rules with roll-to-roll tools, then zig-zag fold it 500-1000 times, with metallized fold-crease edges forming vertical bus bars. Density comes from folding rather than lithography, compressing tens of square metres into a few cm3.
why: Volumetric bits from roll-to-roll tools at ~1/50 the capital of a litho fab, with no wafer and no EUV. Honest density: ~1.7e7 bits/cm2 per layer gives ~2 GB per cm3, viable for capacity tiers, not hot DRAM.

title: Cold substrate, burning film: self-fueled combustion-synthesized dielectrics
idea: Slot-die coat metal-nitrate plus fuel (urea or acetylacetone) inks onto foil or polymer. A ~200 C trigger ignites a self-propagating exothermic reaction inside the film that supplies the energy to form dense AlOx/SiAlOx dielectric while the substrate stays cool.
why: No vacuum ALD tools and no metal-organic Hf/Al precursors; oxides come from abundant nitrates at a fraction of the process energy. It enables low-temperature non-silicon substrates; 5 nm leakage is the open question.

title: Biology builds the cleanroom part: enzyme-deposited conformal oxide films
idea: Immobilize silicatein-like enzymes or diatom-derived peptides on a scaffold so they catalyze water-soluble precursors (silicic acid, titanium bis(ammonium lactato)dihydroxide) into conformal oxide films at room temperature and neutral pH, only where the enzyme sits. Living catalysis, the dirtiest-sounding process, coats deep 3D pores without vacuum, plasma or organometallic precursors.
why: Replaces ALD tools and Hf/Zr organometallic precursors with benign aqueous chemistry on polymer or foil, at very low energy. Protein residue, film density and speed are the risks.

title: Commodity foil annealed into a single crystal: Cu(111) epitaxial substrates
idea: Anneal ordinary battery-grade polycrystalline copper foil near 1030 C in a moving temperature gradient so one seeded grain sweeps the whole roll (abnormal grain growth), giving metre-scale single-crystal Cu(111). It then serves as the epitaxial template and bottom electrode for crystalline dielectric and channel films, so the cheapest polycrystal becomes a perfect crystal by heat alone.
why: Single-crystal substrate area at ~$10/m2 versus ~$1000/m2 for silicon wafers, with no CZ, quartz or polysilicon, from existing battery-foil lines. A matched channel film is the risk.

title: Nothing as the channel: vacuum-gap access transistors that cannot leak
idea: Make each access device a nanoscale sealed-cavity vacuum transistor: a TiN or nanocrystalline-carbon field-emitter tip (no Mo/W) faces a collector across a ~20 nm void, with a surrounding gate modulating emission. With no semiconductor in the channel there is no thermal generation, so off-current is essentially zero and retention is set only by the capacitor dielectric: the emptiest transistor is the best switch.
why: Kills the <=13 fA leakage tail that forces refresh (fact 3), on any substrate (foil, ceramic) with no crystalline semiconductor; refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit) falls toward zero. Emission voltage and on-current are the risks.

title: Metal without crystals: amorphous-iron ribbons as barrier-free substrates
idea: Use melt-spun Fe-B-Si amorphous-metal ribbon (made by the tonne for transformer cores, ~$5/kg, with a U.S. plant) as a flexible conductive substrate and common ground plane. With no grain boundaries for diffusion, the substrate is its own diffusion barrier, and its soft magnetism gives built-in shielding; thin-film memory is built below the ~400-450 C crystallization limit.
why: No silicon wafer; abundant Fe/B/Si from domestic production, no separate barrier films, and substrate cost per m2 ~1/100 of a wafer. Wheel-side roughness and thermal budget are the risks.

title: Ice as the etch tool: freeze-cast templates for capacitor pores
idea: Directionally freeze a water slurry of nickel or carbon nanoparticles on a cold-plate substrate so growing ice lamellae push the particles into vertical walls, then sublimate the ice and sinter. The result is a conductive bottom-electrode scaffold of aligned pores with aspect ratio >100, to coat with dielectric and plate: frozen water digs the holes.
why: Replaces plasma hole etch (fluorocarbons, hardmask, EUV) with water and cold on non-silicon substrates, at near-zero chemical cost. ~10-30x area gain fits decoupling and embedded capacitors now; cell-scale pores need ~100 nm control.

title: Fossil algae as nanofab: diatom frustules as capacitor scaffolds
idea: Culture a single diatom species, whose silica shells carry repeatable ~200 nm pore lattices, or sort U.S. diatomaceous earth, and settle the valves face-down onto a metal-foil electrode. Convert the silica to silicon by magnesiothermic reduction, then coat it conformally so every valve becomes hundreds of parallel high-area capacitor pores: random biology delivers the nano-order litho is paid to make.
why: Nanostructured capacitor area from abundant biological silica with no etch, hardmask or EUV, at very low energy. It suits large-area capacitors first; a random placement tolerant architecture is needed for cells.

title: Metal and silicon trade places: aluminum-induced layer exchange on foil
idea: Sputter aluminum, then amorphous silicon, onto a foil or ceramic substrate with a thin AlOx interlayer. Annealing at ~450 C drives the silicon through the aluminum to grow a continuous large-grain (10-50 um) polysilicon film underneath while the aluminum is pushed to the top, stripped and recycled: the layers swap. Grains far larger than cells put most transistors in single crystals, and the film seeds low-temperature epitaxial thickening.
why: Crystalline silicon channels with no wafer, CZ, quartz or laser-crystallization tools, from abundant aluminum at <500 C. Al doping of the film (~1e18) must be compensated to control leakage.

title: Memory made by non-memory industries: open substrate-agnostic thin-film PDK
idea: Fund an open thin-film memory process design kit and qualification suite whose cell (low-temperature TFT plus planar or rolled capacitor) is defined by electrical windows rather than by substrate. Steel-coil coaters, battery-foil makers, disk-media sputter houses and PV lines can then certify as memory foundries on their own substrates, so the memory industry grows by not needing a memory fab.
why: Unlocks large, depreciated, partly U.S. coating capacity and non-silicon substrates for capacity-tier memory, cutting capital per added bit ~10x versus a DRAM fab. Device performance gates which tiers it serves.

title: Bullets make perfect holes: ion-track-etched templates for capacitor arrays
idea: Irradiate a 3-5 um polyimide layer on any substrate with swift heavy ions from a cyclotron. Each ion leaves a straight latent damage track that etches in NaOH into a 20-50 nm pore with aspect ratio >100; plating electrode and dielectric into the pores gives each cell's storage node ~30-100 random parallel nanotube capacitors, averaging out count noise. Radiation damage becomes the precision tool.
why: Aspect ratio >100 with no plasma etch, fluorocarbons, hardmask or EUV, from polymer and caustic soda; a beamline processes ~m2/hour. Poisson spread (~10-18%) needs margin.
